title: Imbalanced Gray‐Green Infrastructure Closely Parallels Extreme Rainfall‐Flood Resilience Inequality Between Mainstream and Tributary Cities in the Pearl River Basin, Southern China
content:
Abstract

Climate change and rapid urbanization are intensifying flood risks, making unequal gray-green infrastructure (GGI) provision a growing concern for extreme rainfall-flood resilience (ERFR). However, how GGI inequality corresponds with ERFR differences between mainstream and tributary cities remains insufficiently understood. Using the 2025 Typhoon Wutip period as a fixed regional extreme-event observation window, this study quantified GGI inequality and examined basin-scale ERFR differentiation in southern China's Pearl River Basin (PRB). Representing GGI through drainage networks and aggregate urban green-space provision, we combined the Gini coefficient with a machine-learning-based “flood sensitivity-infrastructure vulnerability” framework to map basin-wide ERFR and examine GGI-ERFR relationships among 23 representative cities across hydrological and developmental contexts. Results revealed pronounced inequality in GGI provision. Mainstream cities generally exhibited higher green-space ratios and drainage-network densities, whereas tributary cities had more limited built-up area-based infrastructure provision. Correspondingly, ERFR exhibited marked spatial differentiation, with higher values concentrated in urban clusters, including the Pearl River Delta, and lower values more widely distributed across inland mountainous tributary areas. Built-up area-based GGI indicators showed the most pronounced inequality (Gini>0.70 $\text{Gini} > 0.70$) and were strongly associated with ERFR (ρ=0.82–0.84 $\rho =0.82\mbox{--}0.84$; p<0.001 $p< 0.001$). Together, GGI concentration corresponded closely with the spatially heterogeneous distribution of ERFR across mainstream and tributary settings. These findings highlight the importance of directing infrastructure investment toward under-resourced tributary areas and provide insights for hydrologically differentiated resilience governance in rapidly urbanizing river basins.
